linkedin-optimization-recruiter-seo.core: Recruiters search LinkedIn by keywords, titles, skills and location. Your profile is a search result: a headline with role and key technologies, an About section with outcomes, experience bullets with metrics, and skills matching target roles decide whether you appear and get messaged.

first_principles.problem: A strong SRE gets no inbound messages because their headline says 'Engineer at Acme'.

analogy.title: A shop listing on a search engine
analogy.story: Without the right keywords and a clear description, nobody finds the shop.
analogy.breaks: Shops pay for ads; profile visibility is earned through relevance and activity.

example.title: Rewriting a headline
flow: After: 'Senior SRE | Kubernetes, Terraform, Observability | Cut incidents 60%'

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Appears in searches for SRE + Kubernetes.

check.q: Why put technologies in your LinkedIn headline?
check.a: Recruiters search by keywords, and the headline is prominent in search ranking and results.

the-engineering-blog-proof-of-work.core: Writing about problems you've solved is public proof of skill: it shows depth, communication and judgement, compounds through search over years, and clarifies your own thinking. Posts on real debugging stories, migrations and lessons learned beat generic tutorials.

first_principles.problem: Claims on a résumé are hard to verify; candidates look interchangeable.
truths: Content is discoverable long after posting.

analogy.title: An artist's portfolio
analogy.story: Anyone can say they paint; the portfolio shows it.
analogy.breaks: Portfolios show final work; good posts also show the messy reasoning.

example.title: A high-impact post
flow: 'How we cut p99 latency 70% by fixing connection pooling'

check.q: What kind of post tends to demonstrate expertise best?
check.a: Specific, data-backed accounts of real problems you solved and what you learned.

public-speaking-the-expert-halo.core: Speaking at meetups and conferences creates an 'expert halo': audiences assume speakers are authorities, which brings opportunities, network and credibility. Start small (internal tech talks, local meetups), tell a story with a clear takeaway, and reuse talks across venues.

first_principles.problem: An expert engineer is invisible outside their team.
truths: Talks reach many people at once.

analogy.title: A chef doing a cooking demo
analogy.story: Watching someone cook live convinces you they're an expert far more than a menu does.
analogy.breaks: Cooking demos are visual; tech talks need clear storytelling to engage.

example.title: From internal to conference
flow: Internal lunch talk on an outage
CFP accepted at a regional conference

check.q: What's a low-risk first step into public speaking?
check.a: An internal tech talk or a local meetup.

github-profile-the-portfolio.core: A GitHub profile is a code portfolio: pinned repos with clear READMEs, tests and real use cases, plus meaningful contributions to open source. Quality and clarity beat green-square streaks, and a few polished, relevant projects say more than dozens of abandoned ones.

first_principles.problem: A profile full of forked tutorials and empty repos signals nothing.
derivation: Write **READMEs**: what, why, how to run, demo.

analogy.title: A shop window
analogy.story: Display your best few items beautifully, not everything in the stockroom.
analogy.breaks: Shop windows are static; repos show activity history and collaboration.

example.title: Polishing one project
flow: Used by 3 teams → noted in README

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A reviewer understands it in 30 seconds.

check.q: What's the most important file in a portfolio repo?
check.a: The README, because it's what reviewers read first.

networking-without-cold-outreach.core: The best networks are built by giving value in public: helping in communities, writing, speaking, contributing to open source and staying in touch with former colleagues. Opportunities then come through warm introductions, which convert far better than cold messages.

first_principles.problem: Cold LinkedIn messages to strangers get ignored.
truths: People help those they know and trust.

analogy.title: A village where everyone knows the helpful neighbour
analogy.story: When the neighbour needs something, people offer before being asked.
analogy.breaks: Villages are small; online communities let goodwill scale widely.

example.title: A referral path
flow: Answer Terraform questions in a community Slack for months
Interview starts at the hiring manager

check.q: Why do referrals outperform cold applications?
check.a: They carry trust from someone the company knows, so candidates get prioritised attention.
